title: El Niño: Indonesia fire emissions in 2026 ‘on track’ to match record for this century - Carbon Brief
gist: Indonesian fires had emitted 76m tonnes of carbon by 7 September 2026, tracking the 2015 season that ultimately produced 333MtC, driven by an El Niño that began in June 2026 and is projected to be one of the most intense on record. The new burning frontier has shifted east to Papua and Papua New Guinea while Sumatra stays quiet, and experts cannot yet show that Indonesia's post-2015 peatland restoration push is suppressing fires.

insights.claim: Fires in Indonesia had produced 76m tonnes of carbon in 2026 as of 7 September, according to the Global Fire Emissions Database.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: A hard mid-season baseline for sizing haze, air-quality and palm-oil supply disruption risk in south-east Asia.
insights.quote: Data from the Global Fire Emissions Database reveals that, as of 7 September, fires in Indonesia produced 76m tonnes of carbon (MtC) in 2026.

insights.claim: The 2026 Indonesian fire trajectory matches 2015, when 2.6m hectares burned and total emissions reached 333MtC.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: 2015 is the usable analogue for modelling downside scenarios in regional aviation, tourism, health systems and agricultural commodities.
insights.locator: This puts 2026 on the same trajectory as 2015

insights.claim: Parts of Indonesia including the eastern province of Papua are burning more than they ever have, according to Wageningen University researcher Guido van der Werf.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Record burning in a region with little prior fire history signals geographic expansion of the risk beyond historically monitored provinces.
insights.quote: burning more than they’ve ever burned
insights.locator: Parts of the country – including the eastern province of Papua

insights.claim: The 1997 Indonesian fire season generated carbon emissions equivalent to 13-40% of all global fossil-fuel emissions that year, per published research.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Shows a single national land-use event can move the global carbon budget, complicating any corporate or sovereign net-zero accounting anchored to fossil emissions alone.
insights.locator: Research has estimated that the record 1997 fire season

insights.claim: CO2 emissions from the 2015 south-east Asian fires, which primarily burned Indonesia, exceeded the EU's total fossil-fuel emissions that year, and the resulting haze has been linked to more than 100,000 premature deaths across the region.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Quantifies both the climate and mortality tail-risk of a repeat season — a driver of emergency policy responses and cross-border political friction.

themes.theme: El Niño as amplifier, not cause

insights.claim: The El Niño that began in June 2026 is expected to last into 2027 and is projected by scientists to be one of the most intense on record.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: A multi-quarter climate driver with knock-on effects on Asian agriculture, hydropower and commodity prices well into 2027.
insights.locator: Scientists are projecting that this year’s El Niño

insights.claim: El Niño does not directly cause most Indonesian fires but acts as a major amplifier by creating hotter and drier conditions that make fires easier to ignite, faster to spread and harder to control, according to peatland lead Nisa Novita of Yayasan Konservasi Alam Nusantara.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Ignition is human and structural, so the controllable variable is land-use policy rather than weather — that is where enforcement risk sits for palm oil and pulp buyers.
insights.quote: major amplifier by creating hotter and drier conditions, making fires easier to ignite, spread faster and much harder to control

insights.claim: Fire is normal in Indonesia's August-to-November dry season, but 2026's scale is far beyond what is seen in a typical year or even in previous El Niño years, according to Copernicus Climate Change Service senior scientist Mark Parrington.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Sets the seasonal window — the risk is not yet peaked, with October and November still ahead.
insights.quote: We do normally see fire around this time of year, but nowhere near the scale that we’ve seen this year, or indeed any of the previous El Niño years
insights.locator: Dr Mark Parrington, a senior scientist from the Copernicus

insights.claim: Indonesian fires cluster where land has been cleared and peatland drained for agriculture and palm oil plantations, which leaves a dry, highly flammable landscape during droughts.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Ties fire exposure directly to plantation supply chains — a traceability and reputational risk channel for palm oil offtakers.
insights.locator: Studies have shown that fires in Indonesia often occur

insights.claim: Indonesia's fires are unusually emissions-intensive because canal development for agriculture drops the water table in tropical peatlands, drying the peat so the soil itself becomes fuel that can smolder underground.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Explains why Indonesian burn-area does not map linearly to emissions — drainage state, not hectares, is the variable to monitor.
insights.quote: Unlike fires in dry ecosystems, peat fires can smolder underground, so the soil itself becomes readily available fuel.
insights.locator: Novita explains that Indonesia’s fires are heavily emissions-intensive

insights.claim: Indonesia's institutional response to fires has been reactive and is now partially unwound: a moratorium on forest and peatland conversion licences followed the 1997-98 fires, an official peatland restoration agency was created after 2015 and given a mangrove mandate in 2021, but that agency was dissolved in 2025.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Dismantling the dedicated restoration body just before a major El Niño is a governance signal worth pricing into Indonesian land-use and sovereign ESG assessments.

insights.claim: Extensive peatland restoration has been credited with reducing fire numbers during the 2019 El Niño, but the 2026 data does not yet show a clear benefit from recent restoration efforts.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Undercuts the assumption that restoration investment has durably de-risked Indonesian fire seasons — a caution for carbon-credit and nature-based-solutions exposure.
insights.quote: I had hoped that this year Indonesia would be relatively quiet, even though we have a big El Niño…You could argue if those regulations worked, then this wouldn’t be a big fire [season], even though it [has been] very dry.
insights.locator: Van der Werf says it remains unclear from the 2026 fire data

insights.claim: Papua and neighbouring Papua New Guinea are the new deforestation-and-fire frontiers, repeating what Sumatra went through 20 years ago, while Sumatra itself has had a quiet 2026 fire season.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Frontier displacement means monitoring and supply-chain screening built for Sumatra and Kalimantan may miss where the damage is now occurring.
insights.quote: Papua [a region of Indonesia] and [neighbouring country of] Papua New Guinea – those are the new frontiers. They are basically going through the same thing that Sumatra went through 20 years ago.
insights.locator: This is maybe the case in Sumatra

insights.claim: Whether 2026 exceeds 2015 depends on the duration of this year's El Niño event and the effectiveness of recent peatland conservation efforts.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Two observable variables to track — ENSO duration forecasts and water-table/restoration data — determine the severity outcome.
insights.locator: Van der Werf says the scale of this year’s fires

insights.claim: A researcher at an Indonesian conservation NGO openly questions whether the country is still underestimating the risk posed by degraded peatlands in the face of a new El Niño.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Domestic expert doubt suggests further regulatory tightening or emergency intervention is plausible if the season worsens.
insights.quote: We have learned and improved…But the question is: is it enough? Or are we still underestimating the risk that degraded peatlands pose, especially when we face another El Niño?
